text: Chapter five: Rome. When Wren is the emperor.
Two thousand years ago, Rome paid its soldiers in silver coins called denarii. Under the first emperor, Augustus, they were almost pure silver.
Rome ran on its army. A dying emperor reportedly told his sons: keep the soldiers rich, never mind anyone else.
Soldiers cost more silver than the empire had. So emperors did what Wren did: melt the coins, add cheap copper, stamp out more.
By the year two hundred, coins were about half silver. By two seventy, under five percent: copper, with a thin silver skin.
In Roman Egypt, a sack of wheat cost about eight drachmas in the year one hundred. Prices crept up for a long time, then leapt: by three hundred, about three hundred.
Picture savings worth a year of bread, back then. By three hundred, the same sum bought about ten days. Nobody stole a coin. The emperor just made more.
In three hundred and one, Emperor Diocletian blamed greedy sellers and capped over a thousand prices and wages. Charge more, and you could die.
A writer of the time says blood was spilled over small things, and people were too scared to sell. The law was finally dropped.
Wren needed luck to find a cave of pentaja. An emperor owned one. It was called the mint. Next: is there money with no cave at all?
